questions.stem: An electric bell is ringing inside a bell jar. As the air is gradually pumped out, the sound fades away although the hammer is still seen to strike. This shows that

options.text: sound requires a material medium for its transmission
sound travels faster in a vacuum
the bell stops vibrating in a vacuum

questions.explanation: Sound is carried by compressions and rarefactions of the particles of a medium. Removing the air removes the particles, so there is nothing left to pass the disturbance from the bell to the jar wall, and no sound reaches the observer.

distractorRationale.b: Sound does not travel through a vacuum at all, so no speed can be assigned to it there
distractorRationale.c: The hammer is still clearly seen striking, so the bell is definitely still vibrating
distractorRationale.d: Sound is longitudinal, and in any case the experiment shows the need for a medium, not the type of wave

questions.stem: The pitch of a musical note is determined by its
questions.explanation: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds, and it rises as the frequency of the vibration rises. Tightening a guitar string raises its frequency and therefore its pitch, while the loudness stays the same.

distractorRationale.c: Speed is fixed by the medium and is the same for all notes in the same air
distractorRationale.d: Wavelength does change with pitch, but the property the ear responds to is the frequency, which stays the same in every medium

questions.stem: The approximate range of frequencies audible to a normal human ear is
questions.explanation: A healthy young ear responds from about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Frequencies below this range are infrasound and those above are ultrasound, which is used in medical scanning and echo-sounding.

distractorRationale.a: The upper limit is a hundred times too low; a 200 Hz note is a low hum, well inside the range
distractorRationale.c: The lower limit excludes audible bass notes and the upper limit lies in the ultrasound region
distractorRationale.d: This whole range is ultrasound, which humans cannot hear at all

questions.stem: A man claps his hands and hears the echo from a wall 0.50 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, calculate his distance from the wall. Give your answer in metres.
questions.explanation: The sound travels to the wall and back, so $2d = vt = 340 \times 0.50 = 170\ \text{m}$, giving $d = 85\ \text{m}$. Omitting the factor of 2 would wrongly give 170 m.

questions.stem: A girl stands 165 m from a high cliff and shouts. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, calculate the time after which she hears the echo. Give your answer in seconds.
questions.explanation: Total path travelled by the sound $= 2 \times 165 = 330\ \text{m}$. Time $= \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}} = \frac{330}{330} = 1.0\ \text{s}$. Using only 165 m would give 0.5 s, which is the one-way time.

questions.stem: A drummer strikes a drum harder without changing anything else. The sound produced will have
questions.explanation: Striking harder gives the drum skin a larger amplitude of vibration while its natural frequency stays the same. Larger amplitude means more energy carried and therefore a louder sound, with no change in pitch.

distractorRationale.a: Pitch depends on the frequency, which is set by the size and tension of the drum skin, not by how hard it is hit
distractorRationale.c: Wave speed depends only on the medium, so a louder sound travels no faster
distractorRationale.d: Wavelength depends on speed and frequency, both unchanged here

questions.stem: In which of the following media does sound travel fastest?
questions.explanation: Sound travels fastest where particles are closely packed and the forces between them are strong, because the disturbance is passed on more quickly. Steel gives about 5000 m/s, compared with roughly 1500 m/s in water and 340 m/s in air.

distractorRationale.a: Gas molecules are far apart, so air gives the slowest transmission of the three real media
distractorRationale.b: Water is faster than air but much slower than a solid such as steel
distractorRationale.d: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum at all, so its speed there is not merely slow but undefined

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.25 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency. Give your answer in hertz.
questions.explanation: In a closed pipe the fundamental fits a quarter wavelength into the tube, so $\lambda = 4L = 4 \times 0.25 = 1.0\ \text{m}$. Then $f_0 = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{340}{1.0} = 340\ \text{Hz}$. Equivalently $f_0 = \frac{v}{4L}$.

questions.stem: An open pipe of length 0.34 m resonates in its fundamental mode. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, calculate the fundamental frequency. Give your answer in hertz.
questions.explanation: An open pipe has antinodes at both ends, so the fundamental fits half a wavelength into the tube: $\lambda = 2L = 0.68\ \text{m}$. Then $f_0 = \frac{v}{\lambda} = \frac{340}{0.68} = 500\ \text{Hz}$. Using the closed-pipe formula $\frac{v}{4L}$ would give half this value.

questions.stem: A boy standing 255 m from a cliff shouts and hears the echo 1.5 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in the air. Give your answer in metres per second.
questions.explanation: The sound covers the distance to the cliff and back, so the total path is $2 \times 255 = 510\ \text{m}$. Speed $= \frac{510}{1.5} = 340\ \text{m/s}$. Using 255 m alone would give 170 m/s, only half the true speed.
